title: How to Verify a Private Investigator License in Florida Before You Hire
description: Learn how to verify a Florida private investigator and agency license, understand Class C versus Class A, and spot warning signs before hiring.

html:
Hiring a private investigator often begins with a sensitive problem: suspected fraud, a missing person, a family matter, workplace misconduct, or evidence needed for a legal case. Before you share names, documents, locations, or payment information, take a few minutes to verify the investigator’s Florida license. It is a simple check, and it tells you much more than a badge-shaped logo or the word "licensed" on a website.

The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, commonly called FDACS, licenses and regulates private investigative firms and individuals under Chapter 493, Florida Statutes. The important detail is that Florida distinguishes between the person doing investigative work and the agency offering that work to the public. A careful client checks both.

How Do You Verify a Private Investigator License in Florida?

Start at the official FDACS Search for a Licensee page. Do not depend on a screenshot sent by the investigator, a directory listing, or a search-engine result. Those can be old, incomplete, or connected to someone with a similar name.

  1. Choose the individual search to check the person who will perform or supervise the investigation.
  2. Choose the agency search to check the company accepting the assignment, signing the agreement, or receiving your payment.
  3. Search by the exact legal name or license number provided in the written proposal.
  4. Compare the result with the name on the contract, invoice, website, and payment instructions.
  5. Review the license class and current status shown by FDACS. If anything is unclear, pause and ask the provider to explain the mismatch before you hire.

FDACS provides separate searches because an individual record and an agency record answer different questions. Searching only the company name does not identify the license held by the investigator assigned to your matter. Searching only the individual does not confirm that the business taking your money is licensed as an agency.

What Is the Difference Between a Class C and Class A License?

A Class C license applies to an individual private investigator. FDACS states that any individual who performs the services of a private investigator must have this license. Its published requirements include qualifying experience and an examination covering the laws and responsibilities that apply to the profession.

A Class A license applies to a private investigative agency: the person or business that engages in business as an agency. FDACS also states that a Class A license is valid for only one location. In everyday terms, Class C answers "Is this individual licensed to work as a private investigator?" Class A answers "Is this business licensed to operate as a private investigative agency?"

You may also see other classifications. A Class CC holder is an intern who works under the direction and control of an authorized sponsor. Agency managers can hold Class M or MA licenses, while a qualifying Class C or M licensee may be designated as manager under FDACS rules. Those classifications are legitimate, but they are not interchangeable. Confirm the role the person will actually perform and which agency is responsible for the work.

What Information Should Match in the FDACS Search?

Compare the search result with the documents in front of you. The legal name should make sense in relation to the person or company you contacted. The license class should fit the role. The status should not be expired, suspended, or otherwise inconsistent with a claim that the provider is ready to begin work. If the business uses a trade name, ask for the licensed legal entity behind it.

The FDACS search help identifies A as the prefix for a private investigative agency and C as the prefix for a private investigator. Enter the number exactly as the search requests. If a number produces no useful result, try the exact name and contact FDACS rather than assuming a formatting problem proves the license is valid.

A small spelling difference may have an innocent explanation, such as a legal entity operating under a registered business name. A different person, unrelated company, wrong license class, or unexplained payment recipient deserves more caution. Verification is not about finding a perfect marketing name; it is about establishing a clear chain between the licensed agency, the assigned investigator, the agreement, and the money.

What Are Warning Signs Before You Hire?

  • The provider refuses to give you an individual or agency license number.
  • The number belongs to a different person or company and there is no clear, documented relationship.
  • The provider shows only a Class C individual license but cannot identify the Class A agency accepting the case.
  • The contract uses one business name while payment is requested by an unrelated person or entity.
  • You are pressured to pay immediately before receiving a written scope, rates, expense terms, and cancellation policy.
  • The investigator promises a guaranteed result, guaranteed admissibility, or access to private databases or accounts through questionable methods.
  • The provider discourages you from confirming information with FDACS.

One concern does not automatically establish misconduct. It does mean you should slow down, ask direct questions, and keep written records. A professional investigator should understand why a client wants to verify credentials before discussing a confidential assignment.

What Should You Ask After the License Check?

A valid license is the starting point, not the entire hiring decision. Ask who will handle the work, which tasks may be subcontracted, what jurisdictions are involved, and how out-of-state fieldwork will be assigned. Confirm the objective, lawful scope, estimated hours, hourly rates, retainer, expenses, reporting schedule, and stopping point before work begins.

Ask how sensitive records will be received, stored, shared, and destroyed. If the matter could lead to litigation, discuss evidence preservation and reporting requirements with your attorney. An investigator can document facts and explain methods, but should not guarantee that evidence will be admitted or that an investigation will produce a particular outcome.

Finally, pay attention to how the consultation feels. Clear answers, realistic limits, a written agreement, and respect for privacy are stronger signals than dramatic claims. License verification reduces avoidable risk; thoughtful scoping determines whether the investigator is a good fit for the actual problem.

Verify First, Then Discuss the Assignment

Use the official FDACS individual and agency searches before sending confidential files or paying a retainer. Save the information you reviewed with your intake records, and ask about any difference between the search result and the proposal. When you are ready, request a confidential consultation to discuss the facts, legal boundaries, location, deadline, and budget. No ethical investigator can promise a result, but a properly documented engagement gives the work a sound beginning.
